explanations.C: Correct. The order is: identify the contract, identify the performance obligations, determine the transaction price, allocate that price, and recognise revenue as each obligation is satisfied.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Allocation is step four and cannot precede identification of the obligations.

cfa_fra.stem: A software company sells a licence and one year of support for a bundled price of USD 900. The standalone selling prices are USD 800 for the licence and USD 400 for support. Revenue allocated to the licence is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 800 ignores the bundle discount, which must be spread across both obligations in proportion to standalone prices.
explanations.A: Correct. Allocation = 900 x (800 / 1,200) = USD 600 to the licence and USD 300 to support.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 900 assigns the whole transaction price to one of two distinct performance obligations.

cfa_fra.stem: Variable consideration is included in the transaction price only to the extent that it is:

options.A: highly probable that a significant reversal of cumulative revenue will not occur.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Incorrect. Certainty is a higher bar than the standard requires and would defer nearly all variable amounts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cash receipt is not the recognition trigger under an accrual-based model.
explanations.A: Correct. The constraint on variable consideration limits recognition to the amount for which a significant reversal is highly probable not to occur; the estimate uses the expected value or most likely amount.

cfa_fra.stem: An entity recognises revenue over time rather than at a point in time when:

options.B: the asset created has no alternative use to the entity and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date.
options.C: the contract price exceeds USD 1 million.
options.A: the contract term is longer than twelve months.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Correct. This is one of the three over-time criteria, alongside the customer simultaneously receiving and consuming the benefits, and the entity creating or enhancing an asset the customer controls.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Contract size is irrelevant to the timing criteria.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Duration alone does not determine whether control transfers over time.

cfa_fra.stem: Under IFRS 15, an assurance-type warranty (a promise that the product meets agreed specifications) is accounted for as:

options.A: a separate performance obligation with revenue allocated to it.
options.B: a provision, with the estimated cost accrued when the product is sold.
options.C: a reduction of the transaction price.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Incorrect. Only a service-type warranty, which the customer could purchase separately, is a distinct performance obligation.
explanations.B: Correct. An assurance warranty is not a separate service; the expected cost of honouring it is accrued as a liability under IAS 37 in the period of sale.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Warranty costs are an expense, not a price adjustment.

cfa_fra.stem: Incremental costs of obtaining a contract, such as a sales commission that would not have been incurred had the contract not been won, are:

options.B: capitalised as an asset if the entity expects to recover them, and amortised as the related revenue is recognised.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Incorrect. Immediate expensing is permitted only under a practical expedient when the amortisation period would be one year or less.
explanations.B: Correct. IFRS 15 requires capitalisation of recoverable incremental acquisition costs, amortised on a basis consistent with the transfer of the related goods or services.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Only consideration payable to the customer reduces the transaction price.

cfa_fra.stem: A customer pays USD 100,000 today for equipment that will be delivered in two years. The prevailing discount rate is 6%. The seller should:

options.B: recognise USD 100,000 of revenue on delivery.
options.C: recognise a contract liability that accretes interest expense, with revenue on delivery exceeding USD 100,000.
options.A: recognise USD 100,000 of revenue immediately on receipt of cash.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Incorrect. This ignores the significant financing component embedded in the two-year advance payment.
explanations.C: Correct. Where a contract contains a significant financing benefit to the seller, the liability is accreted at the discount rate and the interest is recognised as a financing cost, so revenue at delivery exceeds the cash received.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Cash receipt precedes satisfaction of the performance obligation.

cfa_fra.stem: A retailer sells goods with an unconditional right of return. At the point of sale, the retailer should:

options.B: recognise revenue only for the amount it expects to be entitled to, with a refund liability for expected returns.
options.C: defer all revenue until the return window expires.
options.A: recognise the full invoice amount as revenue.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Correct. Expected returns are variable consideration; the entity recognises revenue net of expected returns, a refund liability, and an asset for the right to recover the returned goods.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Full deferral is inappropriate when returns can be reliably estimated.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Recognising gross revenue overstates the amount the entity expects to be entitled to.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following best describes the matching principle?

options.A: Expenses are recognised when cash is paid.
options.B: Expenses are recognised in the same period as the revenues they help generate.
options.C: Expenses are recognised evenly over the fiscal year.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Incorrect. That is the cash basis, which accrual accounting rejects.
explanations.B: Correct. Costs with a direct causal link to revenue — cost of goods sold, sales commissions, warranty costs — are recognised in the period the related revenue is recognised.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Straight-line allocation applies only to period costs with no identifiable revenue association.

cfa_fra.stem: Which cost is a period cost rather than a product cost?
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.C: Incorrect. Production supervision is manufacturing overhead, capitalised into inventory.
explanations.A: Correct. General and administrative costs have no identifiable association with specific units of output and are expensed in the period incurred.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Direct materials are a product cost capitalised into inventory until sale.

cfa_fra.stem: A company reports revenue of USD 1,000, cost of sales of USD 600, SG&A of USD 200, depreciation of USD 80, and interest of USD 40. EBITDA is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 200 is operating profit (EBIT), which is after depreciation.
explanations.C: Correct. EBITDA = revenue - cost of sales - SG&A = 1,000 - 600 - 200 = USD 200 before depreciation; adding back the USD 80 of depreciation already deducted gives USD 280.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 120 deducts interest as well, which EBITDA excludes by construction.

cfa_fra.stem: On a multi-step income statement, gross profit is:

options.C: operating profit less interest and tax.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Correct. Gross profit isolates the direct margin on goods and services sold, before operating overheads.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Deducting all operating expenses yields operating profit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Deducting interest and tax from operating profit yields net income.

cfa_fra.stem: A company grants employees share options that vest over four years. The related compensation expense is:

options.A: recognised in full on the grant date.
options.B: recognised over the four-year vesting period, based on the grant-date fair value.
options.C: never recognised, because no cash changes hands.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Incorrect. The employee has not yet rendered the service that the award compensates.
explanations.B: Correct. Grant-date fair value is expensed over the requisite service period, with a corresponding credit to equity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Share-based payment is a real cost of employment even though it is settled in equity.

cfa_fra.stem: An analyst notes that a company's cost of sales excludes depreciation on manufacturing equipment, which is reported on a separate line. Relative to a peer that includes it, this company's reported gross margin will be:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Correct. Excluding a genuine cost of production from cost of sales inflates gross profit; the analyst must reclassify before comparing gross margins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Removing a cost from the numerator's deduction raises, not lowers, gross profit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Presentation choices within the income statement directly affect subtotal-based margins.

cfa_fra.stem: A company changes from the straight-line to the double-declining balance method of depreciation. Under IFRS this is:

options.A: a change in accounting estimate applied prospectively.
options.B: a change in accounting policy applied retrospectively.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Correct. IAS 16 treats the depreciation method as a reflection of the expected pattern of consumption of benefits, so a change to it is a change in estimate applied prospectively.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Unlike an inventory cost formula, the depreciation method is not treated as a policy for this purpose.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The prior method was acceptable, so nothing was in error.

cfa_fra.stem: A company recognises USD 40,000 of bad debt expense by increasing its allowance for doubtful accounts. The effect on the accounting equation is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Correct. Net receivables (an asset) fall via the contra account, and the expense reduces retained earnings within equity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The allowance is a contra-asset, not a liability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An expense reduces equity; it cannot increase it.

cfa_fra.stem: A telecommunications company sells a handset together with a 24-month service plan. Under IFRS 15, relative to the previous practice of treating the handset as a marketing cost, the company will most likely report:

options.A: more revenue at contract inception and less over the service period.
options.B: less revenue at contract inception and more over the service period.
options.C: the same revenue pattern, since total consideration is unchanged.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Correct. The handset is a distinct performance obligation, so a portion of the total consideration is allocated to it and recognised on delivery, front-loading revenue relative to the old treatment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is the opposite of the allocation effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Total consideration is unchanged, but its timing across periods is not.

cfa_fra.stem: An input method for measuring progress toward complete satisfaction of a performance obligation would use:

options.C: units delivered relative to total units promised.
options.A: costs incurred relative to total expected costs.
options.B: surveys of performance completed to date.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.C: Incorrect. Units delivered is an output measure.
explanations.A: Correct. Input methods measure the entity's efforts or inputs consumed — labour hours, machine hours, or the cost-to-cost approach.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Appraisals and surveys of results achieved are output measures.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following would most likely cause reported revenue to be recognised on a gross rather than net basis?

options.C: The entity has inventory risk before the good is transferred to the customer.
options.A: The entity earns a fixed commission per transaction.
options.B: The supplier sets the price charged to the end customer.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.C: Correct. Bearing inventory risk is a key indicator that the entity controls the good before transfer and is therefore the principal, reporting gross revenue.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A fixed commission is a classic agent indicator.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lack of pricing discretion points to agent status.

cfa_fra.stem: A company recognises revenue when goods are shipped, but the customer takes control only on delivery, which averages three weeks later. This practice most likely:

options.A: accelerates revenue recognition relative to the standard.
options.B: defers revenue recognition relative to the standard.
options.C: has no effect, since the goods are eventually delivered.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Correct. Recognising on shipment when control passes on delivery pulls revenue into an earlier period, inflating current results and building unbilled or in-transit balances.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Shipment precedes delivery, so recognition is earlier, not later.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Period-to-period cut-off is precisely what recognition timing governs.

cfa_fra.stem: A company reports 'operating income' that includes a USD 30 million gain on the sale of a factory. For forecasting purposes an analyst should:

options.B: include the gain, since management classified it as operating.
options.C: exclude the gain from the sustainable operating base.
options.A: annualise the gain over the next four quarters.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Incorrect. Management's classification is not binding on the analyst, and disposal gains are not a repeatable source of operating profit.
explanations.C: Correct. A one-off disposal gain must be stripped out before extrapolating operating income, and the associated loss of the factory's future output considered.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Spreading a non-recurring gain forward compounds the error.

cfa_fra.stem: Net income is USD 900,000 and the weighted average number of common shares is 300,000. During the year the company also declared USD 60,000 of dividends on non-cumulative preferred shares. Basic EPS is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 3.00 omits the preferred dividend deduction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 3.20 adds the preferred dividend to the numerator instead of deducting it.

cfa_fra.stem: For cumulative preferred shares, the amount deducted in computing basic EPS is:

options.A: only the dividends actually declared during the period.
options.B: the dividends for the period whether or not they were declared.
options.C: nothing, since cumulative dividends are a liability.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Incorrect. That rule applies to non-cumulative preferred shares.
explanations.B: Correct. Cumulative preferred dividends accrue to the preferred holders regardless of declaration, so the full periodic entitlement reduces income available to common shareholders.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Undeclared cumulative dividends are generally not recognised as a liability, but they still reduce the EPS numerator.

cfa_fra.stem: A company effects a 3-for-1 stock split in the final month of the fiscal year. In computing the weighted average share count for EPS, the split is:

options.B: applied only to the final month.
options.C: applied retroactively to the beginning of the earliest period presented.
options.A: ignored, because no cash was received.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Incorrect. Time-weighting applies to share issues for consideration, not to splits.
explanations.C: Correct. Splits and stock dividends change the number of shares without changing resources, so all prior share counts and per-share figures are restated for comparability.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The share count changes and must be reflected.

cfa_fra.stem: When a company has multiple potentially dilutive securities, diluted EPS is computed by:

options.A: including all of them simultaneously regardless of effect.
options.B: ranking them from most to least dilutive and including each only while EPS continues to fall.
options.C: including only the single most dilutive security.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Incorrect. Including antidilutive securities would overstate diluted EPS and is prohibited.
explanations.B: Correct. Securities are sequenced by their incremental effect on EPS and added one at a time; inclusion stops once a security would raise EPS.
explanations.C: Incorrect. All dilutive securities are included, not just one.

cfa_fra.stem: A company with a net loss has 200,000 outstanding employee share options that are in the money. In computing diluted EPS, these options are:

options.C: included, increasing the loss per share.
options.A: excluded, because they would be antidilutive when there is a loss.
options.B: included only to the extent of the intrinsic value.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.C: Incorrect. Increasing the denominator against a negative numerator would make the loss per share smaller, which is antidilutive.
explanations.A: Correct. With a loss, any increase in the share count reduces the reported loss per share, so all potentially dilutive securities are excluded.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no partial-intrinsic-value inclusion method.

cfa_fra.stem: The treasury stock method assumes that proceeds from the assumed exercise of options are used to:

options.A: repay debt at the market interest rate.
options.B: repurchase shares at the average market price for the period.
options.C: pay a special dividend to existing shareholders.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Incorrect. Debt repayment is the assumption in the if-converted method for convertible debt, and even there it is the interest that is added back.
explanations.B: Correct. The net incremental share count equals the shares issued on exercise less the shares that could be repurchased with the exercise proceeds at the average market price.
explanations.C: Incorrect. No dividend assumption is involved.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following is most likely to be classified as an unusual or infrequent item within continuing operations?

options.B: A gain from the sale of a discontinued business segment.
options.C: A loss from the write-off of obsolete equipment following a plant restructuring.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Incorrect. That gain is presented within discontinued operations, net of tax.
explanations.C: Correct. Restructuring-related write-offs are unusual in nature but remain part of continuing operations and are disclosed separately, pre-tax.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Depreciation is an ordinary recurring expense.

cfa_fra.stem: A company's revenue grew 8% while its accounts receivable grew 25% and days sales outstanding lengthened from 45 to 55 days. The most appropriate analytical conclusion is that:

options.C: revenue quality has deteriorated and collection risk has increased.
options.A: the company has improved its credit terms to customers at no cost.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.C: Correct. Receivables outrunning sales and a lengthening collection period point to looser credit, channel loading, or recognition ahead of collectibility — all reasons to discount reported revenue growth.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Extending credit consumes working capital and raises default exposure; it is never costless.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pattern suggests revenue may be overstated relative to cash economics, not understated.

cfa_fra.stem: A manufacturer capitalises USD 5 million of costs into inventory that a peer expenses immediately. Relative to the peer, in the year of the outlay this manufacturer reports:

options.B: higher gross profit and higher current assets.
options.C: lower gross profit and lower current assets.
options.A: higher gross profit and lower current assets.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Correct. Deferring the cost into inventory keeps it out of cost of sales until the goods are sold, raising gross profit, and it sits on the balance sheet as a current asset.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Both effects run the other way.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Capitalisation increases, not decreases, current assets.

cfa_fra.stem: An entity that presents a 'statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income' as two separate statements must:

options.B: begin the second statement with profit or loss for the period.
options.C: present other comprehensive income before profit or loss.
options.A: omit the total for comprehensive income.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Correct. When the two-statement presentation is used, the statement of comprehensive income starts with the profit or loss figure carried down from the first statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. OCI is presented after profit or loss, not before it.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The total of comprehensive income must be presented.

cfa_fra.stem: Which OCI item is subsequently reclassified ('recycled') to profit or loss?

options.A: Revaluation surplus on property, plant, and equipment.
options.B: Cumulative translation adjustment on disposal of the foreign operation.
options.C: Remeasurements of a defined benefit pension plan under IFRS.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Incorrect. The revaluation surplus is transferred within equity to retained earnings; it never passes through profit or loss.
explanations.B: Correct. On disposal of a foreign operation, the accumulated translation adjustment relating to it is reclassified from equity to profit or loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect. IAS 19 remeasurements are never recycled.

cfa_fra.stem: A company reports revenue of USD 500 million and cost of sales of USD 350 million in Year 1, and USD 600 million and USD 438 million in Year 2. The change in gross margin is closest to:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Incorrect. The margin fell; it did not rise.
explanations.C: Correct. Year 1 gross margin = 150 / 500 = 30.0%; Year 2 = 162 / 600 = 27.0%; the margin contracted by 3.0 percentage points despite revenue growth of 20%.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Both revenue and cost grew, but cost grew faster in percentage terms.

cfa_fra.stem: An analyst separating a company's revenue growth into volume and price effects is performing:

options.C: a decomposition that isolates whether growth is being bought with discounting.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.B: Incorrect. Common-size analysis scales line items; it does not decompose a single line into drivers.
explanations.C: Correct. Volume-versus-price decomposition reveals whether top-line growth reflects genuine demand or is being purchased through price cuts that will show up later in margin.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Solvency concerns the capital structure and debt service.

cfa_fra.stem: A company sells a product for USD 500 that includes two years of free servicing with a standalone value of USD 100. At the point of sale, revenue recognised is:

options.B: the portion of USD 500 allocated to the product based on relative standalone selling prices.
options.C: USD 400, the invoice price less the service value.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Income Statement

explanations.A: Incorrect. Recognising the full amount ignores the unsatisfied service obligation.
explanations.B: Correct. The service is a distinct performance obligation, so the transaction price is allocated between product and service on relative standalone selling prices, and the service portion is recognised over the two years.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Simply subtracting the standalone service price is the residual approach, which is permitted only in limited circumstances; the general rule is relative allocation.

cfa_fra.stem: An asset is classified as current when it is expected to be realised within:

options.A: twelve months of the reporting date only.
options.B: the entity's normal operating cycle or twelve months, whichever is longer.
options.C: the entity's normal operating cycle only.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.A: Incorrect. A strict twelve-month test would misclassify inventory and receivables in long-cycle industries such as shipbuilding or distilling.
explanations.B: Correct. IAS 1 uses the longer of the operating cycle and twelve months, which is why aged inventory can still be current in some industries.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Assets held primarily for trading and cash are current regardless of the operating cycle.

cfa_fra.stem: A bank or insurer commonly presents its balance sheet:

options.C: in order of liquidity rather than as a current/non-current classification.
options.B: with liabilities before assets in every jurisdiction.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.C: Correct. IAS 1 permits a liquidity-based presentation where it provides more relevant information, which is typical for financial institutions whose operating cycle is not meaningful.
explanations.A: Incorrect. No framework prescribes alphabetical ordering.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ordering conventions vary, but that is a matter of jurisdictional custom, not a defining feature of financial institutions.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following qualifies as a cash equivalent?

options.B: A 90-day treasury bill purchased two months before maturity.
options.C: Ordinary shares in a listed company that trade in a deep market.
options.A: A two-year corporate bond that the company intends to sell next month.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Correct. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible to known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of value change — conventionally an original maturity of three months or less.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Equity investments are excluded because their value is not insignificantly variable.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The classification test is based on maturity at acquisition, not on management's selling intention.

cfa_fra.stem: Under IFRS 9, a debt instrument is measured at amortised cost when the business model is to hold it to collect contractual cash flows and:

options.B: the instrument is quoted in an active market.
options.C: those cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest.
options.A: the instrument matures within twelve months.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Incorrect. Whether a quoted price exists does not determine the measurement category.
explanations.C: Correct. Both conditions must hold: the hold-to-collect business model and the solely-payments-of-principal-and-interest (SPPI) characteristic of the cash flows.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Maturity affects current/non-current presentation, not the measurement category.

cfa_fra.stem: An equity investment held for trading is measured at:

options.B: fair value through profit or loss.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.A: Incorrect. Amortised cost is available only for debt instruments meeting the SPPI and hold-to-collect conditions.
explanations.B: Correct. Equity investments default to FVPL; an irrevocable election to present changes in OCI is available only for equities not held for trading.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A cost-based measurement for equity investments is not permitted under IFRS 9.

cfa_fra.stem: Under IAS 37, a provision is recognised when there is a present obligation from a past event, an outflow of resources is probable, and:

options.B: the amount can be estimated reliably.
options.C: the obligation is legally enforceable in court.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Correct. All three conditions must be met; if the amount cannot be reliably estimated the item is disclosed as a contingent liability instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Constructive obligations arising from an established pattern of practice also qualify.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A formal demand is not a recognition criterion.

cfa_fra.stem: A contingent liability that is possible but not probable is:

options.C: recognised as a provision at its expected value.
options.A: disclosed in the notes but not recognised.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.C: Incorrect. Recognition requires that the outflow be probable.
explanations.A: Correct. Possible obligations, and present obligations that fail the probability or measurement test, are disclosed unless the possibility of outflow is remote.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Silence is appropriate only when the possibility of an outflow is remote.

cfa_fra.stem: A contingent asset whose realisation is probable is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.A: Incorrect. Recognition occurs only when realisation is virtually certain, at which point it ceases to be contingent.
explanations.B: Correct. The asymmetric treatment reflects prudence: probable inflows are disclosed, probable outflows are recognised.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Probable inflows warrant disclosure.

cfa_fra.stem: A company breaches a covenant on its long-term loan at the reporting date, giving the lender the right to demand immediate repayment. Absent a waiver obtained before the reporting date, the loan is classified as:

options.B: non-current, because the contractual maturity is unchanged.
options.C: current, because the entity does not have an unconditional right to defer settlement beyond twelve months.
options.A: equity, until the lender exercises the right.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Incorrect. Classification follows the right to defer settlement, not the original maturity schedule.
explanations.C: Correct. A breach that makes the liability payable on demand at the reporting date forces current classification, which can abruptly destroy the current ratio.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A borrowing is never reclassified to equity.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following is a component of shareholders' equity?
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.C: Correct. Non-controlling interest is the portion of a subsidiary's equity not attributable to the parent, presented within total equity but separately from owners of the parent.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Deferred tax liabilities are obligations, presented as non-current liabilities.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Provisions are liabilities of uncertain timing or amount.

cfa_fra.stem: Current assets are USD 480 and current liabilities are USD 300. Working capital is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.A: Correct. Working capital = current assets - current liabilities = 480 - 300 = USD 180.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 1.60 is the current ratio, a unitless multiple rather than an amount.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 780 adds the two figures.

cfa_fra.stem: Total assets are USD 2,000, total liabilities are USD 1,400, and there are 50 million shares outstanding. Book value per share is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.C: Correct. Equity = 2,000 - 1,400 = USD 600; book value per share = 600 / 50 = USD 12.00.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 40.00 divides total assets by shares outstanding, ignoring liabilities.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 28.00 divides total liabilities by shares outstanding.

cfa_fra.stem: A company purchases a competitor for USD 500 million. The fair value of identifiable net assets acquired is USD 380 million, of which USD 60 million is a customer relationship intangible not previously recognised by the target. Goodwill recognised is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Correct. Goodwill = 500 - 380 = USD 120 million. The customer relationship is already included in the USD 380 million of identifiable net assets.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 180 million double-counts by excluding the customer intangible from identifiable net assets.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 60 million is the customer relationship intangible, which is identifiable and therefore not goodwill.

cfa_fra.stem: Research costs incurred by a pharmaceutical company are:

options.C: capitalised as an intangible asset under both IFRS and US GAAP.
options.A: expensed as incurred under both IFRS and US GAAP.
options.B: capitalised under IFRS and expensed under US GAAP.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.C: Incorrect. Neither framework permits capitalisation of research, as distinct from development.
explanations.A: Correct. Research — the pursuit of new knowledge without a demonstrated feasible product — is expensed under both frameworks.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The IFRS/US GAAP divergence concerns development costs, not research costs.

cfa_fra.stem: A company acquires a patent for USD 3 million with a legal life of 20 years and an expected economic life of 8 years. Annual amortisation on a straight-line basis with no residual value is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 150,000 uses the 20-year legal life, but amortisation follows the shorter useful life over which benefits are consumed.
explanations.C: Correct. 3,000,000 / 8 = USD 375,000 per year.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Immediate write-off would apply only if the asset failed the recognition criteria.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following transactions leaves total assets unchanged?

options.C: Paying a supplier in cash to settle an account payable.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.C: Incorrect. Cash and payables both fall, so total assets and total liabilities each decrease.
explanations.A: Correct. Cash decreases and PP&E increases by the same amount; the composition of assets changes but the total does not.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cash and liabilities both rise, increasing total assets.

cfa_fra.stem: On a common-size balance sheet, an increase in 'inventory as a percentage of total assets' from 12% to 20% over three years most likely warrants investigation of:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Incorrect. Dividends are a financing decision unrelated to inventory composition.
explanations.C: Correct. Inventory absorbing a growing share of the asset base, absent a matching sales increase, is a leading indicator of write-down risk and weakening demand.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The tax rate has no direct bearing on the inventory share of assets.

cfa_fra.stem: Retained earnings increase by:

options.B: net income plus proceeds from share issuance.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.C: Correct. Retained earnings roll forward as opening balance plus net income less dividends declared, adjusted for any prior-period corrections.
explanations.A: Incorrect. OCI accumulates in AOCI, a separate equity component, not in retained earnings.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Share issuance proceeds go to contributed capital.

cfa_fra.stem: An unrealised gain on an equity investment for which the entity has made the irrevocable FVOCI election is:

options.B: recognised in OCI and never reclassified to profit or loss, even on disposal.
options.C: deferred until the investment is sold.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.A: Incorrect. That is the FVPL treatment, which is the default for equity investments.
explanations.B: Correct. For the equity FVOCI election, gains and losses stay in OCI permanently; on disposal the cumulative amount may be transferred within equity but never through profit or loss. Only dividend income hits profit or loss.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The asset is remeasured to fair value each reporting date.

cfa_fra.stem: An analyst comparing the book value of equity with the market capitalisation of a technology company observes that market value is many times book value. The most likely explanation is that:

options.C: internally generated intangibles such as brand and technology are not recognised on the balance sheet.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Incorrect. Impairment would reduce book value further but does not explain why the market pays a large premium.
explanations.C: Correct. Historical-cost accounting and the prohibition on recognising internally generated intangibles mean the balance sheet systematically omits the assets that drive value in asset-light businesses.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A large book-to-market gap is a structural feature of the measurement model, not evidence of error.

cfa_fra.stem: A liability for employee bonuses earned in the current year but payable next March is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.A: Correct. The service has been rendered and the obligation exists at the reporting date, so an accrual is recognised even though payment falls in the next period.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A prepaid expense is a payment made in advance of consuming the benefit — the mirror image.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The obligation is present and measurable, not contingent.

cfa_fra.stem: Under IAS 16, if an asset previously written down through profit or loss is revalued upward, the increase is:

options.A: recognised in profit or loss to the extent it reverses the prior decrease, with any excess in OCI.
options.B: recognised entirely in profit or loss.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.C: Incorrect. OCI treatment applies only to the portion exceeding the previously expensed decrease.
explanations.A: Correct. The symmetry rule ensures the income statement recovers what it previously bore, and only genuine new appreciation bypasses profit or loss.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Routing the entire increase through profit or loss would overstate earnings.

cfa_fra.stem: Deferred revenue increases when:

options.A: a customer pays before the entity performs.
options.B: the entity performs before the customer pays.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.A: Correct. Cash in advance creates a contract liability, released to revenue as the performance obligation is satisfied.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Performing before payment creates a receivable or contract asset.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A write-off reduces receivables against the allowance.

cfa_fra.stem: A rising balance of deferred revenue at a software company is most often interpreted by analysts as:

options.B: a warning sign of deteriorating demand.
options.C: a positive indicator of contracted future revenue.
options.A: evidence that the company has overstated its revenue.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Incorrect. Falling deferred revenue is the warning sign, since it signals a shrinking contracted backlog.
explanations.C: Correct. Deferred revenue is cash already collected against obligations still to be performed, so it represents revenue with high visibility.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Deferred revenue is precisely the amount not yet recognised as revenue.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following would increase both total assets and total equity?

options.C: Borrowing on a five-year term loan.
options.A: Issuing shares in exchange for a patent.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.C: Incorrect. Borrowing raises assets and liabilities, leaving equity unchanged.
explanations.A: Correct. The patent is recognised as an intangible asset and contributed capital rises by the same amount.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A buyback reduces both cash and equity.

cfa_fra.stem: An asset held for sale under IFRS 5 is measured at:

options.B: the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, and is not depreciated.
options.A: historical cost less accumulated depreciation, unchanged.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Correct. Once the held-for-sale criteria are met, depreciation ceases and the asset is written down if fair value less costs to sell is below carrying amount.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Depreciation stops because the carrying amount will be recovered through sale rather than use.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Reclassification triggers the specific IFRS 5 measurement.

cfa_fra.stem: A company's balance sheet shows total debt of USD 600 million and total equity of USD 400 million. Its debt-to-capital ratio is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Incorrect. 1.50 is the debt-to-equity ratio, 600 / 400.
explanations.C: Correct. Debt-to-capital = debt / (debt + equity) = 600 / 1,000 = 0.60.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.40 is the equity share of total capital.

cfa_fra.stem: Accrued interest payable on a bond is presented as:

options.A: a reduction of the bond's carrying amount.
options.B: a current liability, separate from the bond principal.
options.C: a component of interest expense in equity.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.A: Incorrect. The carrying amount of the bond reflects principal and unamortised discount or premium, not accrued coupon.
explanations.B: Correct. Interest accrued but unpaid at the reporting date is a short-term obligation reported among current liabilities.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Expenses are never presented within equity.

cfa_fra.stem: Which measurement basis is used for trade receivables under IFRS 9?

options.B: Fair value through profit or loss.
options.C: Amortised cost, less an expected credit loss allowance.
options.A: Historical invoice value with no allowance.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Incorrect. Ordinary trade receivables are held to collect contractual cash flows and are not measured at FVPL.
explanations.C: Correct. IFRS 9 requires a lifetime expected credit loss allowance for trade receivables, recognised from initial recognition rather than only when a loss event has occurred.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The expected credit loss model requires an allowance even for a currently performing book.

cfa_fra.stem: Under IFRS 9's expected credit loss model, relative to the previous incurred-loss model, loss allowances are generally:

options.A: unchanged in both timing and amount.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Correct. Forward-looking expected losses are provided for from initial recognition rather than waiting for objective evidence of impairment, which front-loads and enlarges allowances.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Later recognition is the criticism the expected loss model was designed to address.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The change in model materially altered both timing and magnitude, particularly for lenders.

cfa_fra.stem: A company reports 'other assets' equal to 18% of total assets with no further breakdown. The analyst should:

options.C: treat the lack of disaggregation as a disclosure weakness and seek to understand the composition.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Incorrect. Nearly a fifth of the balance sheet cannot be assumed immaterial.
explanations.C: Correct. A large undisaggregated residual defeats the purpose of a classified balance sheet and is itself a governance and reporting-quality signal.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Substituting a guess for evidence is not an acceptable adjustment.

cfa_fra.stem: The primary limitation of the balance sheet for assessing a company's economic value is that:

options.C: it is prepared only once every three years.
options.A: many assets are carried at historical cost and important economic resources are not recognised at all.
options.B: it does not reconcile to the income statement.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.C: Incorrect. Balance sheets are presented at every annual and interim reporting date.
explanations.A: Correct. Historical-cost measurement, plus non-recognition of internally generated intangibles and human capital, means carrying amounts frequently diverge from economic value.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Retained earnings link the two statements; articulation is not the limitation.

cfa_fra.stem: A company sells receivables to a third party without recourse. The most likely balance-sheet effect is:

options.B: receivables are derecognised and cash increases, improving the receivables turnover ratio.
options.C: receivables remain on the balance sheet with an offsetting liability.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Correct. Where substantially all risks and rewards transfer, the receivable is derecognised — which also flatters DSO and turnover, so the analyst should adjust for the sold balances before drawing conclusions about collection efficiency.
explanations.C: Incorrect. That is the treatment for a sale with recourse or one failing derecognition, which is accounted for as secured borrowing.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A sale converts receivables into cash, not the reverse.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following is presented within equity but is NOT attributable to the parent's shareholders?
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.B: Incorrect. AOCI attributable to the parent is part of the parent's equity.
explanations.C: Correct. NCI represents the outside shareholders' claim on consolidated subsidiaries; it sits inside total equity but outside equity attributable to owners of the parent, which matters when computing ROE.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Share premium is contributed capital of the parent.

cfa_fra.stem: An analyst computing return on equity for a consolidated group with a large non-controlling interest should use:

options.A: net income attributable to the parent divided by equity attributable to the parent.
options.B: total consolidated net income divided by total equity including NCI.
options.C: total consolidated net income divided by equity attributable to the parent.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Balance Sheet

explanations.A: Correct. Numerator and denominator must refer to the same claimants; mixing them distorts the ratio.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is internally consistent but answers a different question — the return to all equity claimants — and is not the parent-shareholder ROE.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This mismatches a group-wide numerator with a parent-only denominator, systematically overstating ROE.

cfa_fra.stem: Under US GAAP, dividends received from an investment are classified as:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. US GAAP requires both interest received and dividends received to be operating inflows. IFRS permits either operating or investing.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Investing classification of dividends received is an IFRS option, not the US GAAP rule.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Only dividends paid are financing, and only under US GAAP without an alternative.

cfa_fra.stem: Under IFRS, income taxes paid are classified as operating unless:

options.B: the entity elects financing classification for all taxes.
options.C: the tax can be specifically identified with an investing or financing activity.
options.A: the amount exceeds 10% of pre-tax income.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no blanket election; the default is operating.
explanations.C: Correct. IAS 7 allows allocation to investing or financing where the tax cash flow can be specifically identified with such an activity, for example tax on a disposal gain.
explanations.A: Incorrect. No quantitative threshold governs the classification.

cfa_fra.stem: A company reports the following: purchases of PP&E USD 200, proceeds from sale of PP&E USD 50, purchases of investments USD 80, proceeds from sale of investments USD 30. Cash flow from investing is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.A: Incorrect. USD -360 treats the proceeds as outflows rather than inflows.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD +80 nets only the proceeds against each other.

cfa_fra.stem: A company issues debt of USD 300, repays debt of USD 120, pays dividends of USD 60, and repurchases shares for USD 40. Cash flow from financing is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Incorrect. USD +180 omits the dividend and buyback outflows.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD -80 reverses the sign of the net result.

cfa_fra.stem: Income tax expense is USD 100, taxes payable increased by USD 15, and the deferred tax liability increased by USD 10. Cash taxes paid are:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. Cash taxes = expense - increase in taxes payable - increase in DTL = 100 - 15 - 10 = USD 75.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 125 adds both increases, which reverses their effect on cash.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 100 is the accrual expense, not the cash outflow.

cfa_fra.stem: Operating expenses are USD 400, prepaid expenses increased by USD 20, and accrued liabilities increased by USD 15. Cash paid for operating expenses is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. Cash paid = 400 + 20 (cash spent ahead of the expense) - 15 (expense recognised ahead of cash) = USD 405.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 395 reverses both adjustments.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 435 adds the accrued liability increase instead of subtracting it.

cfa_fra.stem: Cash at the beginning of the year is USD 120, CFO is USD 300, CFI is USD -250, and CFF is USD -30. Ending cash is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 700 sums the absolute values of all flows.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 100 omits the opening balance treatment or misapplies a sign.

cfa_fra.stem: In an indirect-method reconciliation, a loss on the sale of equipment is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Correct. The loss reduced net income but consumed no operating cash; it is added back, and the full sale proceeds appear as an investing inflow.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Deducting would double-count the loss.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Every non-operating and non-cash item in net income must be removed.

cfa_fra.stem: Under the indirect method, an increase in accounts payable is:

options.A: added to net income, because the company has deferred cash payment.
options.B: deducted from net income, because liabilities have grown.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.A: Correct. Expenses recognised but not yet paid mean cash outflow was less than accrual expense, so the increase is a source of cash.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Deducting would understate operating cash.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Trade payables arise from operating activity, not financing.

cfa_fra.stem: Share-based compensation expense is treated in an indirect-method statement of cash flows as:

options.C: a non-cash add-back to net income.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. The expense is settled in equity instruments rather than cash, so it is added back — though an analyst should not treat it as costless, since it dilutes existing shareholders.
explanations.A: Incorrect. No cash leaves the entity when the award is granted or vests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. No asset is acquired.

cfa_fra.stem: An investor accounts for an associate under the equity method and recognises USD 40 of income while receiving USD 15 of dividends. In the indirect-method reconciliation, the net adjustment to net income is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. The full USD 40 of equity income is non-cash and is removed; the USD 15 dividend actually received is added back, giving a net deduction of USD 25.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Equity income exceeds the cash received, so the adjustment reduces rather than increases operating cash.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Deducting the full USD 40 ignores the USD 15 of cash actually collected.

cfa_fra.stem: A company acquires a subsidiary for USD 500 in cash, and the subsidiary holds USD 60 of cash at the acquisition date. The investing outflow reported is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 500 ignores the cash acquired, which partly offsets the outflow.
explanations.C: Correct. Acquisitions are reported net of cash and cash equivalents acquired: 500 - 60 = USD 440.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 560 adds the acquired cash to the outflow.

cfa_fra.stem: The effect of exchange rate changes on cash held in foreign currency is:

options.C: included within cash flow from operations.
options.A: presented as a separate reconciling item, outside the three activity categories.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Incorrect. Including it would misstate operating cash generation.
explanations.A: Correct. IAS 7 requires the effect of exchange rate changes on cash balances to be presented separately so that the three activity totals reconcile to the change in cash.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Omitting it would break the reconciliation to the opening and closing cash balances.

cfa_fra.stem: CFO is USD 300 and average total assets are USD 2,000. The cash return on assets is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. Cash return on assets = CFO / average total assets = 300 / 2,000 = 15.0%.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 6.7% inverts the ratio.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 1.5% is off by a factor of ten.

cfa_fra.stem: CFO is USD 300, interest paid is USD 40, and taxes paid are USD 60. Cash-based interest coverage is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. (CFO + interest paid + taxes paid) / interest paid = (300 + 40 + 60) / 40 = 10.0 times.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 7.5x omits both add-backs, using 300 / 40.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 8.5x adds back interest only, giving 340 / 40.

cfa_fra.stem: The reinvestment ratio, computed as CFO divided by cash paid for long-term assets, measures the company's ability to:

options.A: repay its long-term debt from operations.
options.B: fund asset replacement and growth from internally generated cash.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.A: Incorrect. That is the debt coverage ratio, CFO divided by total debt.
explanations.B: Correct. A ratio above 1.0 means operations fully fund capital spending; persistently below 1.0 signals reliance on external financing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. That is the dividend payment ratio, CFO divided by dividends paid.

cfa_fra.stem: A mature, profitable company would most typically show:

options.A: positive CFO, negative CFI, and negative CFF.
options.B: negative CFO, positive CFI, and positive CFF.
options.C: positive CFO, positive CFI, and positive CFF.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.A: Correct. Operations generate cash, some of which is reinvested in assets and the remainder returned to capital providers through dividends, buybacks, and debt repayment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That pattern — burning operating cash while selling assets and raising capital — describes a company in distress.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Positive investing and financing alongside positive operations usually indicates a build-up of cash ahead of a specific event, not a steady state.

cfa_fra.stem: A start-up reports negative CFO, negative CFI, and large positive CFF. This pattern is best interpreted as:

options.C: a company funding growth and operating losses with external capital.
options.A: a company in the mature phase of its life cycle.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. The signature of an early-stage growth company: operations consume cash, assets are being built, and investors are supplying the funding. The analytical question is runway, not wrongdoing.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Mature companies generate operating cash and return capital.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The pattern is entirely consistent with a legitimate growth-stage business.

cfa_fra.stem: Net income is USD 200, depreciation is USD 60, the deferred tax liability increased by USD 12, a gain on asset sale was USD 25, and net working capital increased by USD 35. CFO is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. 200 + 60 + 12 - 25 - 35 = USD 212. Depreciation and the deferred tax increase are non-cash add-backs; the gain is removed and the working capital build is a use of cash.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 262 adds the gain instead of removing it and mishandles the working capital change.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 232 omits the working capital adjustment.

cfa_fra.stem: Under IFRS, a company may classify dividends paid as an operating outflow. Relative to a US GAAP peer, this choice will result in:

options.B: lower reported CFO for the IFRS company.
options.C: higher reported CFO for the IFRS company.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Correct. The US GAAP company always reports dividends paid in financing, so the IFRS company that puts them in operating reports lower CFO for the same economics.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Moving an outflow into operating reduces, not raises, CFO.
explanations.A: Incorrect. This is precisely a case where reported CFO is not comparable without adjustment.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following is a non-cash transaction requiring separate disclosure?

options.B: Conversion of convertible bonds into common shares.
options.C: Payment of an income tax instalment.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Correct. A conversion restructures the balance sheet — debt down, equity up — with no cash movement, so it is disclosed outside the three activity sections.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A tax instalment is a cash outflow, normally operating.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Collection is a cash operating inflow.

cfa_fra.stem: Gross PP&E rose from USD 800 to USD 950 and the company disposed of assets with an original cost of USD 70. Cash paid for PP&E, assuming all purchases were for cash, is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 150 is the net change in gross PP&E, which understates purchases because it is after the disposals.
explanations.B: Correct. Purchases = ending gross - beginning gross + cost of disposals = 950 - 800 + 70 = USD 220.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 80 subtracts the disposals instead of adding them back.

cfa_fra.stem: Accumulated depreciation rose from USD 300 to USD 340, and accumulated depreciation on assets disposed of during the year was USD 55. Depreciation expense for the year is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 40 is the net movement, which is after removing the accumulated depreciation on disposals.
explanations.B: Correct. Expense = ending balance - beginning balance + accumulated depreciation removed on disposal = 340 - 300 + 55 = USD 95.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 15 subtracts rather than adds the disposal adjustment.

cfa_fra.stem: A company reports CFO of USD 500, capital expenditure of USD 180, and dividends paid of USD 90. Free cash flow after dividends is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Correct. 500 - 180 - 90 = USD 230, the discretionary cash remaining after maintaining the asset base and honouring the dividend.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 320 is free cash flow before dividends.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 410 deducts only the dividend.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following would cause CFO to rise without any improvement in underlying operating performance?

options.C: Stretching payment terms with suppliers at the end of the reporting period.
options.A: Increasing the gross margin on products sold.
options.B: Reducing the effective tax rate through improved operations.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. Delaying supplier payments inflates payables and CFO in the current period at the cost of the next one — a classic window-dressing technique that shows up as a jump in days payable outstanding.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A genuine margin improvement is an improvement in performance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sustainable tax efficiency is a real economic gain.

cfa_fra.stem: Securitising and selling trade receivables near the reporting date will most likely:

options.A: increase CFO in the current period.
options.B: decrease CFO in the current period.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.A: Correct. Converting receivables to cash reduces the operating working capital build, boosting CFO — but the benefit is one-off unless the programme keeps growing, and reversing it later depresses CFO.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sale is a source, not a use, of operating cash.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Receivables are an operating asset, so their reduction flows through CFO.

cfa_fra.stem: Cash collected from customers is USD 900, cash paid to suppliers and employees is USD 620, interest paid is USD 30, and taxes paid is USD 55. Using the direct method, CFO is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. 900 - 620 - 30 - 55 = USD 195, assuming interest paid is classified as operating.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 280 stops at cash from customers less operating payments, omitting interest and tax.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 250 omits the taxes paid.

cfa_fra.stem: A common-size cash flow statement scaling each item by total inflows and total outflows is most useful for:

options.C: identifying which activities the company relies on for cash and where it deploys that cash.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Incorrect. The tax rate comes from the income statement and tax note.
explanations.C: Correct. Expressing each source as a share of total inflows and each use as a share of total outflows reveals dependence on borrowing, asset sales, or operations at a glance.
explanations.A: Incorrect. No presentation format forecasts prices.

cfa_fra.stem: Under IFRS, interest received may be classified as:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. IAS 7 permits interest received to be operating or investing, applied consistently. Under US GAAP it must be operating.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Operating-only is the US GAAP requirement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Interest received is never a financing item.

cfa_fra.stem: An analyst observes that a company's CFO has exceeded net income in each of the past five years, with the gap driven mainly by depreciation on a large fixed asset base. This most likely indicates:

options.B: a capital-intensive business with high non-cash charges, not necessarily superior earnings quality.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Correct. A structural depreciation add-back explains the gap; the offsetting question is whether capital expenditure is consuming that cash, which is why free cash flow rather than CFO is the more informative measure here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Aggressive recognition produces the opposite pattern, with net income above CFO.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Strong and stable operating cash generation is not a distress signal.

cfa_fra.stem: Which adjustment is required when converting an indirect-method operating section to the direct method?

options.B: Allocating each accrual-based income statement line to its corresponding cash flow using the related balance sheet accounts.
options.C: Reclassifying investing outflows as operating outflows.
options.A: Removing depreciation from the income statement entirely.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Correct. Each revenue and expense line is converted by adjusting for the change in its associated working capital account — receivables for revenue, inventory and payables for cost of sales, and so on.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The conversion changes presentation within the operating section only.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Depreciation simply does not appear in the direct-method presentation, because no cash line corresponds to it.

cfa_fra.stem: Under US GAAP, when the direct method is used to present operating cash flows, the company must also:

options.C: provide a reconciliation of net income to cash flow from operations.
options.A: present the investing section using the indirect method.
options.B: restate the prior year on a direct basis only.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. US GAAP requires the indirect reconciliation as a supplementary disclosure even when the direct method is presented; IFRS encourages but does not require it.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The direct/indirect distinction applies only to the operating section.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Comparatives follow the same presentation, but no such restriction exists.

cfa_fra.stem: A company classifies a three-year bank overdraft facility drawdown as an operating inflow. An analyst should:

options.A: accept the classification, since management has discretion.
options.B: reclassify it as a financing inflow, since it is borrowed money rather than cash generated by operations.
options.C: reclassify it as an investing inflow.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neither framework gives discretion to classify term borrowings as operating.
explanations.B: Correct. A multi-year drawdown is a financing transaction; leaving it in CFO would misrepresent the company's ability to generate cash internally.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Investing covers acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and investments.

cfa_fra.stem: Inventory decreased by USD 45 and accounts payable decreased by USD 60 during the year. The combined effect on CFO is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Correct. The inventory drawdown is a USD 45 source of cash, while paying down payables is a USD 60 use, for a net USD 15 reduction in operating cash.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 105 treats both movements as sources.
explanations.A: Incorrect. USD 15 with the wrong sign; the payables reduction dominates.

cfa_fra.stem: A company with strong reported net income but repeatedly negative free cash flow and rising debt is best characterised as:

options.C: generating accounting profits that are not converting into distributable cash.
options.A: exceptionally efficient at working capital management.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. Profit that never becomes cash, funded by increasing leverage, is the classic pattern preceding a liquidity event — and it is invisible if the analyst stops at the income statement.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Efficient working capital management would improve, not depress, cash conversion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rising debt to fund a cash shortfall is the opposite of being overcapitalised.

cfa_fra.stem: When a company capitalises development costs rather than expensing them, the effect on reported cash flows is to:

options.B: increase CFO and decrease CFI, with no change in total cash flow.
options.C: increase both CFO and total cash flow.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.B: Correct. The same cash leaves the business either way; capitalisation simply moves the outflow from the operating to the investing section, which is why analysts compare free cash flow rather than CFO across differing policies.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Total cash flow is a fact about the bank account and is unaffected by classification.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Capitalisation raises CFO and makes CFI more negative.

cfa_fra.stem: An analyst wishes to compare the operating cash generation of two companies, one of which capitalises far more of its expenditure. The most comparable measure is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Incorrect. Reported CFO is exactly what the capitalisation policy distorts.
explanations.A: Correct. Deducting capital spending neutralises the operating-versus-investing classification choice and puts both companies on a free-cash-flow basis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Net income is affected by the same policy difference through depreciation and expensing.

cfa_fra.stem: Cash flow to revenue is 12% and the industry median is 20%. This most likely suggests the company:

options.C: converts a smaller portion of each sales dollar into operating cash than its peers.
options.A: has a higher gross margin than its peers.
options.B: pays lower taxes than its peers.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. The ratio measures cash conversion efficiency; a below-median figure points to weaker margins, heavier working capital absorption, or both.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A higher gross margin would generally support a higher, not lower, cash-to-revenue ratio.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lower tax payments would raise operating cash flow.

cfa_fra.stem: Debt coverage measured as CFO divided by total debt has fallen from 0.35 to 0.12 over three years. The most appropriate conclusion is that:

options.C: the company's ability to service and repay debt from operations has weakened materially.
options.A: the company has become more profitable.
options.B: the company's tax rate has fallen.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.C: Correct. Whether driven by falling CFO, rising debt, or both, the company now needs roughly eight years of operating cash to retire its debt rather than under three.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Profitability is not measured by this ratio, and the trend points the wrong way in any case.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tax rates are not an input to the ratio.

cfa_fra.stem: The single most useful question an analyst can answer from the statement of cash flows that cannot be answered from the income statement is:

options.B: where the company's cash came from and what it was spent on.
options.C: what the company's tax rate was.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Statement of Cash Flows

explanations.A: Incorrect. Profitability is the income statement's purpose.
explanations.B: Correct. Only the cash flow statement reveals the sources and uses of cash — whether growth is self-funded, whether dividends are covered, and whether reported profits are converting into cash.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The effective tax rate is derived from the income statement and tax note.

cfa_fra.stem: Beginning inventory is USD 200, purchases during the year are USD 900, and ending inventory is USD 250. Cost of goods sold is:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.A: Correct. The inventory equation gives COGS = beginning + purchases - ending = 200 + 900 - 250 = USD 850.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 950 adds the ending balance instead of deducting it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 1,350 sums all three figures.

cfa_fra.stem: The specific identification cost formula is most appropriate for:

options.B: large volumes of interchangeable units such as barrels of crude oil.
options.C: inventory items that are not ordinarily interchangeable, such as bespoke machinery or fine art.
options.A: any inventory, at the entity's discretion.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.B: Incorrect. Interchangeable units are costed using FIFO or weighted average.
explanations.C: Correct. IAS 2 requires specific identification for items that are not ordinarily interchangeable and for goods produced and segregated for specific projects.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The choice of formula is not free; it must reflect the nature of the inventory.

cfa_fra.stem: Under which cost formula do periodic and perpetual inventory systems always produce the same cost of goods sold?
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.A: Correct. Under FIFO the oldest costs are charged first regardless of when the calculation is performed, so the timing of the costing has no effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Periodic LIFO uses the latest costs of the whole period, while perpetual LIFO uses the latest costs available at each sale date; the results differ.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Periodic weighted average uses one rate for the period; the perpetual (moving average) recomputes after each purchase.

cfa_fra.stem: In a period of rising prices, a company using FIFO rather than LIFO will report:

options.C: higher gross profit and higher income taxes.
options.A: lower gross profit and lower income taxes.
options.B: higher gross profit and lower income taxes.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.C: Correct. FIFO charges older, cheaper costs to COGS, producing higher gross profit and therefore a larger tax bill in jurisdictions where the book method drives the tax method.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Both effects run the other way.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Higher pre-tax profit cannot produce lower tax at a constant rate.

cfa_fra.stem: In a period of rising prices, a LIFO reporter will show, relative to an otherwise identical FIFO reporter:

options.A: a higher inventory turnover ratio and a lower current ratio.
options.B: a lower inventory turnover ratio and a higher current ratio.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.A: Correct. LIFO produces higher COGS and lower carrying inventory, so turnover (COGS / average inventory) rises on both counts, while the smaller inventory balance depresses current assets and hence the current ratio.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Both effects are stated backwards.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cost formula affects both the numerator and denominator of these ratios.

cfa_fra.stem: An inventory item has a cost of USD 100 and a net realisable value of USD 85. Under IFRS, the required entry is:

options.A: a write-down of USD 15, charged to profit or loss.
options.B: no entry, since the item has not been sold.
options.C: a write-down of USD 15, charged to other comprehensive income.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.A: Correct. Inventory is carried at the lower of cost and NRV, and the write-down is recognised as an expense — usually within cost of sales — in the period it occurs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lower-of-cost-or-NRV test is applied at each reporting date, not at sale.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inventory write-downs never go to OCI.

cfa_fra.stem: An inventory item with an original cost of USD 100 was written down to a carrying amount of USD 85. In the next period its net realisable value recovers to USD 110. Under IFRS the carrying amount becomes:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inventory is never written up above original cost.
explanations.B: Correct. The reversal is limited to the amount of the original write-down, so the carrying amount returns to cost of USD 100 — a USD 15 credit to cost of sales.
explanations.C: Incorrect. IFRS requires reversal when NRV recovers; only US GAAP prohibits it.

cfa_fra.stem: A company's current assets are USD 500, including LIFO inventory of USD 200, and current liabilities are USD 250. The LIFO reserve is USD 80. The current ratio adjusted to a FIFO basis is closest to:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.A: Incorrect. 2.00 is the unadjusted LIFO current ratio, 500 / 250.
explanations.B: Correct. FIFO current assets = 500 + 80 = 580; the associated deferred tax is non-current, so the current ratio = 580 / 250 = 2.32.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 1.68 subtracts the reserve from current assets.

cfa_fra.stem: A US GAAP company discloses that its LIFO reserve declined during a year in which its supplier prices rose. This most likely indicates:
cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.A: Correct. With prices rising, the reserve should grow; a decline points to inventory quantities falling and old low-cost layers being charged to COGS, inflating gross profit unsustainably.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A method change would be disclosed as a change in accounting principle, not shown as a shrinking reserve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. US GAAP prohibits reversal of inventory write-downs.

cfa_fra.stem: Goods held on consignment by a retailer on behalf of a manufacturer should be included in the inventory of:

options.B: the retailer, because it has physical possession.
options.C: the manufacturer, because it retains the risks and rewards of ownership.
options.A: neither party, until the goods are sold.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.B: Incorrect. Physical possession does not determine recognition; control and the risks and rewards of ownership do.
explanations.C: Correct. The consignor retains title and bears the risk of unsold goods, so the inventory stays on its balance sheet.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The goods exist and must be recognised by whichever party controls them.

cfa_fra.stem: Which of the following costs is included in the cost of inventory?

options.B: Transport costs of bringing raw materials to the factory.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.A: Incorrect. Selling costs are incurred after the inventory is ready and are period expenses.
explanations.B: Correct. Inward freight is a cost of purchase, along with the purchase price, import duties, and non-recoverable taxes, net of trade discounts and rebates.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Administrative overhead not related to bringing inventories to their present location and condition is expensed.

cfa_fra.stem: Fixed production overhead is allocated to inventory based on:

options.B: actual production volume in the period, however low.
options.C: the normal capacity of the production facilities.
options.A: the maximum theoretical capacity of the facilities.

cfa_fra.origin: CFA Level I | FRA | Inventories

explanations.B: Incorrect. Allocating fixed overhead over an abnormally low volume would capitalise the cost of idle capacity into inventory.
